summary: Seahorse Key lighthouse in the Cedar Keys, Levy County, Florida: lit 1854, discontinued 1915, dark until a replica fourth-order lens relit it in July 2019.

lens.where: replica fourth-order lens installed 2019; the Archive records the original optic as removed

access.note: Landing not permitted 1 March to 1 July (bird nesting). Open houses typically in July and during the October seafood-festival weekend. Boat access from Cedar Key.

visit.note: Tidewater Tours runs boats during open houses (LighthouseFriends). Do not climb the tower outside open houses.

facts.agency: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service (owner); University of Florida Marine Laboratory (manager; leased parcel since 1952)

events.note: Plans approved by the Lighthouse Board in January 1854 (George Meade). Brick tower with keeper's dwelling.
Lit 1 August 1854 by William Wilson with a fourth-order Fresnel lens.
Extinguished at the onset of the Civil War; Union blockade and destruction of military structures on Seahorse Key, January 1862 (LighthouseFriends).
Returned to service 23 August 1866 after repairs (LighthouseFriends).
Charleston earthquake felt at the station 31 August 1886, 9:31 p.m. (keeper's report as printed by LighthouseFriends).
Repairs made necessary by the storm of 28 and 29 September 1896 (Board report); hurricane destroyed many mills and factories in town (LighthouseFriends).
Characteristic changed 20 December 1899; re-established 20 March 1900 (Board report for the fiscal year ended 30 June 1900, scan 29).
Large additions on east and west sides for a Navy wireless telegraph station, 1903 to 1905 (LighthouseFriends).
23 August 1914: keeper Charles H. Gardner rescued a man who had drifted three miles offshore in a rowboat.
Cedar Key National Wildlife Refuge reserved by Hoover (LighthouseFriends).
Seahorse Key made part of the refuge by Executive Order 7484, 6 November 1936 (LighthouseFriends).
Three-acre parcel including the lighthouse leased to the University of Florida for the Seahorse Key Marine Laboratory (LighthouseFriends).
Relit 5 July 2019 with a replica fourth-order fixed/flashing lens; lens installed 20 May 2019 (Gilchrist County Journal); LighthouseFriends credits Artworks Florida with the replica.

notes_for_editor: Story: us-fl-cedar-key.md (about 1,150 words, six chapters). Open disagreements left in the story or flagged here: (a) range: the record gives 4.0 nm; LighthouseFriends says the light could be seen for fifteen miles (unit not stated); the Gilchrist article's 2019 history says ten miles. Not used in the story. (b) Focal plane: LighthouseFriends 75 ft, Archive 74.5 ft (used). Record 4.9 m is wrong (see corrections). (c) Navy wireless additions: LighthouseFriends 1903 to 1905; Wikipedia (lead only, not cited) says 1905. The story uses LighthouseFriends' range. (d) 2019 lens maker: Gilchrist says Fresnel Lenses, LLC built and installed the lens (20 May 2019); LighthouseFriends says Artworks Florida was contracted to build the replica. A Lighthouse Digest search snippet (not fetched, not cited) names Artworks Florida's Dan Spinella. Both may be true (contractor vs builder); not resolved. (e) Funding of the 2019 project: Gilchrist says a Florida Historical grant applied for by UF; LighthouseFriends says about $50,000 from the Florida Historical Board. Not used. Hobday family: the Archive lists Andrew D. Hobday, Catherine Hobday, John P. Hobday and William A. Hobday. The sources read do not say how they were related; the story says so. Keeper names match between the Archive roster and LighthouseFriends' keeper list (no extra stints added). Page checks: the Board's 1900 report entries (characteristic change on scan 29; revolving machinery on scan 141), the 1891-92 sailboat entry (scan 473) and the 1896-97 storm entry (scan 374) were located by phrase in the corpus OCR index; the printed page numbers are not confirmed. Fiscal years: the sailboat entry sits in the report for the fiscal year ended 30 June 1892, the storm entry in the report for the year ended 30 June 1897, the characteristic change in the report for the year ended 30 June 1900. Verification pass corrections: Fillmore was Taylor's successor, so Fillmore himself reserved the island (story and evidence); Wilson's 'just under a year' is LighthouseFriends', not the Archive's; the Archive's 1915 discontinued date belongs to the light, not the wireless station; the 1899 characteristic change cites scan 29, not scan 141. The 1886 earthquake report is not in the local corpus: that passage is footnoted to LighthouseFriends' printing of it. Not used: the Gainesville Sun 2019 article (HTTP 403); the Coast Guard Historian's Cedar Key page (archived copies 403 or no capture); Wikipedia (lead only; its watchtower claim of 1801 is not used, since its cited source was not read). Chronicling America searches for Cedar Keys in Florida papers (1854-1915) returned no usable station page. Access and safety: the island is a federal refuge with a student dormitory in the lighthouse; the story says visits are on open-house days or authorized trips only. Photos: none new.
